Yet the flood didn’t destroy the power of sin over human beings. The city of Babel and the tower were examples of how sin continued. People worked together against God. The tower they built showed how full of pride they were. They wanted to stay in the city of Babel instead of filling the earth. Only when they could no longer speak the same language did they spread throughout the world.

The family lines of Japheth, Shem and Ham show how this happened. These family lines record the beginnings of many people groups.

Genesis continued the record of Noah’s family line through Shem. God chose to work through Shem’s family line in his plan for saving the world. Abram was part of Shem’s family.

The fifth account ({{Genesis 10:1|10:1}}) in Genesis (see study note on 2:4) unites the Table of Nations ({{Genesis 10:2-32|10:2–32}}) and the Babel story ({{Genesis 11:1-9|11:1–9}}) around the theme of scattering the nations ({{Genesis 10:5|10:5}}, {{Genesis 10:18|18}}; {{Genesis 11:4|11:4}}, {{Genesis 11:8-9|8–9}}). The Table of Nations appears before the Babel story, but the Babel event explains how the nations and languages in that list came to exist.

By placing these events in this order, Genesis connects the filling of the earth with the blessing God gave to Noah and his sons (see {{Genesis 9:1|9:1}} and study note). It shows that the growth of the nations comes from God’s blessing.

This order also prepares for Abram’s call ({{Genesis 12:1-3|12:1–3}}). Abram’s call shows God’s answer to the problem seen at Babel ({{Genesis 11:1-9|11:1–9}}), where humans were separated from God. Through Abram, God begins to restore that relationship.

*Now*: The events in {{Genesis 11:1-9|11:1–9}} caused the nations to scatter, as shown in the family histories of {{Genesis 10:2-30|10:2–30}}. Although these events happened in a different order than they are written, the author arranged them this way to help explain things about God's actions and plans more clearly (see study note on 10:1–11:9).

The story of the unfinished tower continues themes from the Table of Nations (chapter {{Genesis 10:1-32|10}}). These themes include language and human unity. The builders wanted independence from God, which recalls the rebellion in the garden of Eden (chapter {{Genesis 3:1-24|3}}). This also helps show why Abram’s faithful response to God is needed (chapter {{Genesis 12:1-20|12}}) during a time of disorder among the nations.

The scattering of the nations also points forward to later warnings given to Israel. God warned that idolatry would lead to their being scattered, and that their cities would be ruined (see {{Leviticus 26:33|Leviticus 26:33}}; {{Numbers 10:35|Numbers 10:35}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:27|Deuteronomy 4:27}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:64|28:64}}; {{Deuteronomy 30:3|30:3}}). 

In the timeline of Genesis, this goes back to an earlier time. It explains how the nations spread out during the time of Peleg (see {{Genesis 10:25|Genesis 10:25}}).

- *journeyed eastward:* See study note on 3:24.

- Shinar (Babylonia) was in southern Mesopotamia, where Nimrod later built his empire and cities (see {{Genesis 10:10|10:10}}; {{Isaiah 11:11|Isaiah 11:11}}; {{Daniel 1:2|Daniel 1:2}}; {{Zechariah 5:11|Zechariah 5:11}}).

- Stone was plentiful in Canaan. In Mesopotamia, stone was rare, so they developed brick-making technology. 

- They made *tar* from bitumen, a natural, waterproof asphalt similar to cement (see {{Genesis 6:14|6:14}}; {{Exodus 2:3|Exodus 2:3}}).

- Far from the original garden ({{Genesis 2:15|2:15}}), the first cities of Genesis represent arrogance ({{Genesis 4:17|4:17}}), tyranny ({{Genesis 10:8-12|10:8–12}}), and evil ({{Genesis 18:20-21|18:20–21}}). The city on the Babylonian plain attracted human pride and idol worship. 

- *a tower that reaches to the heavens:* This was probably a temple-tower (a ziggurat). In ancient Babylonian cities, people considered ziggurats to be sacred mountains where gods came down to earth. Jacob’s dream in {{Genesis 28:12|28:12}} might indicate this idea. 

- *that we may make a name for ourselves:* The tower builders wanted fame through their idol-worshiping ambition. God promised to make Abram famous because of his humble obedience ({{Genesis 12:2|12:2}}).

*came down:* The tower was a human attempt to reach up to God’s realm (God’s dwelling place; see {{Deuteronomy 26:15|Deuteronomy 26:15}}; {{Psalm 2:4|Psalms 2:4}}; {{Psalm 103:19|103:19}}; {{Psalm 115:16|115:16}}). This effort was foolish. God had to “come down” to see what they were building, which shows how small and weak their work really was.
If no one stopped them, the tower builders would become united and ambitious. This would allow human evil to grow in ways that cannot be imagined.

- *Come, let Us go down:* God speaks to his angelic court (see {{Genesis 1:26|1:26}}; {{Genesis 3:22|3:22}}; and study notes). 

- *will not understand one another’s speech:* When people could no longer understand one another, their shared plan to do wrong would stop. Later, at Pentecost, God allowed people to understand many languages. This showed a partial reversal (undoing) of what happened at Babe ({{Acts 2:5-13|Acts 2:5–13}}; see {{Zephaniah 3:9|Zephaniah 3:9}}).

*the LORD scattered them: *In a *s*imilar way, God punished Adam and Eve for trying to become independent of his rule. God punished Cain for murder. Their punishments involved exile and scattering ({{Genesis 3:23|3:23}}; {{Genesis 4:12|4:12}}, {{Genesis 4:14|14}}; {{Genesis 9:19|9:19}}; {{Genesis 10:5|10:5}}, {{Genesis 10:25|25}}, {{Genesis 10:32|32}}).

- *Babel: *The Babylonians saw their city as the home or gateway of the gods. The double meaning at the end of this story shows Babylon's spiritual confusion. 

Babylon became important under Nimrod ({{Genesis 10:10|10:10}}) and later in biblical history (see {{2 Kings 25:1-30|2 Kings 25:1–30}}). Its role as a center of pride and idol worship makes it a symbol for the forces opposed to God in the end times (for example, {{Revelation 14:8|Revelation 14:8}}; {{Revelation 16:19|16:19}}; {{Revelation 18:2|18:2}}). 

- The tower builders gathered together in one place to reach up into God’s realm (God’s dwelling place; {{Genesis 11:3-4|Genesis 11:3–4}}). God came down and scattered them across the earth. In this way, he stopped their idolatrous ambition (their desire to act against him and seek their own glory).

- This account of Shem continues from {{Genesis 10:21-32|10:21–32}}, focusing on the family line leading to Abram. Only Abram and Israel inherit Shem’s God (see {{Genesis 9:26-27|9:26–27}}; {{Deuteronomy 32:8-9|Deuteronomy 32:8–9}}). The Babel story strongly rejects the culture that God called Abram to abandon ({{Genesis 12:1|Genesis 12:1}}; {{Genesis 24:6-7|24:6–7}}). Together with the account of Terah’s descendants ({{Genesis 11:27-32|11:27–32}}), this account of Shem’s line forms a bridge from the universal history of chapters {{Genesis 1:1-11:32|1–11}} to Israel's national history that begins in chapter {{Genesis 12:1-20|12}}. 

Abram was part of the small group that remained faithful after the confusion at Babel.

God chose Abram as an act of grace. Through Abram, God began a new plan. God’s purpose was to bless the whole world, even though the nations had been divided and scattered at Babel ({{Genesis 12:3|12:3}}). 

- *the father of *(or *the ancestor of*): Hebrew family records (genealogies, or lists of ancestors) do not always include every generation.

- *Nahor* was Laban's grandfather. Laban's daughters later married Jacob (chapters {{Genesis 29:1-31:55|29–31}}). 

- *Lot:* See the “Lot” Profile.

This brief section provides a complete summary of Terah’s life and accounts for his other sons and their marriages. It also introduces Lot, Abram’s nephew, who later played an important role. The ancestors, including Terah and his family, were idolatrous, worshiping other gods in Mesopotamia ({{Joshua 24:2|Joshua 24:2}}).

*This is the account*: The Hebrew word is *toledoth* (a term that introduces a new section or family history; see study note on 2:4). This section tells about Terah’s family. 

The details in {{Genesis 11:28-25:11|11:28–25:11}} are about the family line that comes from Terah. The focus is on Abraham and God’s covenant with him.

The passage also highlights Isaac, the promised child. Isaac continued the family line and carried God’s blessing to the next generation.

- Abram received his calling from God in Ur of the Chaldeans ({{Genesis 15:7|15:7}}; {{Acts 7:2-4|Acts 7:2–4}}). This was the main city of Sumer in Mesopotamia near the Persian Gulf. The family had moved there perhaps generations before this calling. Their original home ("country," {{Genesis 12:1|Genesis 12:1}}) was probably near Haran, in the region of Shem's descendants ({{Genesis 11:10-26|11:10–26}}). They settled in Haran after leaving Ur ({{Genesis 11:31|11:31}}). Later, they were described as Arameans ({{Deuteronomy 26:5|Deuteronomy 26:5}}). 

- *native land:* The same Hebrew phrase appears in {{Genesis 12:1|12:1}} ("country"), indicating that Ur, not Haran, was where Abram received his calling (see {{Genesis 15:7|15:7}}; {{Nehemiah 9:7|Nehemiah 9:7}}; {{Acts 7:2|Acts 7:2}}).

- *Sarai* means "princess" in Hebrew. The text does not mention Sarai's parents. This might have been to create suspense in the story of Abimelech. This story reveals her as Abram's half-sister ({{Genesis 20:9-12|20:9–12}}). Later, the law forbade such marriages ({{Leviticus 18:9|Leviticus 18:9}}; {{Leviticus 20:17|20:17}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:22|Deuteronomy 27:22}}). 

- Nahor's wife was Milcah, who was the daughter of Haran and Nahor's niece (see {{Genesis 11:29|Genesis 11:29}}). Her son Bethuel was Rebekah's father. Rebekah became the wife of Abram's son Isaac ({{Genesis 24:10|24:10}}, {{Genesis 24:15|15}}, {{Genesis 24:24|24}}). The name *Milcah* is related to the Hebrew word for "queen." 

In Akkadian, it is a title for the goddess Ishtar, the daughter of the moon god. Terah's name is related to the Hebrew word for "moon." His family probably worshiped Sin, the moon god (see {{Joshua 24:14|Joshua 24:14}}).

Sarai, Rebekah, and Rachel could not have children at first ({{Genesis 25:21|25:21}}; {{Genesis 29:31|29:31}}). Sarai’s case especially shows the tension between what people could see and what God had promised. God had promised to make Abram into a great nation ({{Genesis 12:2|12:2}}). 

Israel began through women who could not bear children. This shows that Israel existed because of God’s power and choice. God gave children to women who were barren (unable to have children), as these passages also show (see also {{1 Samuel 1:2|1 Samuel 1:2}}; {{1 Samuel 2:5|2:5}}; {{Psalm 113:9|Psalm 113:9}}; {{Isaiah 54:1|Isaiah 54:1}}).

- *Terah took:* Abram left Ur because God called him (see study note on 11:28). Yet, the story relates from Terah’s viewpoint, reflecting the ancient Near Eastern culture where the oldest male led the family. This respect for elders is probably why Abram did not go to Canaan alone at that time (see {{Acts 7:2-4|Acts 7:2–4}}). 

- Haran was 885 kilometers (550 miles) northwest of Ur, near the Syrian-Turkish border. Despite the similar name, there is no connection to Terah’s son Haran, who died in Ur ({{Genesis 11:28|11:28}}).

- *Haran* means “caravan.” It was a major trade center where ancient trade routes met. 

- Haran was also famous for moon worship, which Terah’s family probably practiced (see study note on 11:29).
Abram knew that he should leave, but he did not know where he was going. Obedience required faith.
These verses are structured around two commands to Abram: *Leave* and *be a blessing* (see study note on 12:2). Each command is followed by three promises conditioned upon obedience.

- Through Abram's faith and family, God started to restore the blessing. God called Abram from a pagan world to start a new nation. His promises to Abram later became a covenant (chapter {{Genesis 15:1-21|15}}). 

- God's calling of Abram later helped convince the Israelites to leave Egypt and go to the land God promised to Abram. It also reminded the Babylonian exiles of their need to return to their own land (for example, {{Isaiah 51:1-23|Isaiah 51}}).

God made a promise to Abram. Abram was to leave his father’s land and family in Mesopotamia. He was to go to a new land. God would make Abram’s family into a great nation. This meant that there would be many children and grandchildren from Abram’s family line.

God would bless all nations on earth because of Abram. And God would give Abram’s family the land of Canaan to live in.

The stories in Genesis show how God was faithful in keeping his promises to Abram. They show how sometimes Abram was faithful to God and sometimes he wasn’t faithful. He was faithful when he went to Canaan with Sarai, Lot and everything they owned. He was faithful when he refused to grow rich from the king of Sodom. He trusted that God would provide what he needed.

Abram wasn’t faithful when he lied about Sarai to Pharaoh. He didn’t trust God to take care of him in Egypt. Yet God remained faithful to Abram even when Abram wasn’t faithful in return. God protected Abram and Sarai in Egypt and blessed them with riches.

God repeated his promises to Abram after Lot moved to a different area. God gave Abram success when he rescued Lot from the kings who attacked Sodom. After the battle, Melchizedek recognised that God was taking care of Abram. Melchizedek blessed Abram in God’s name.

- *make your name great:* Abram gained the fame that the builders of the tower of Babel wanted for themselves (see {{Genesis 11:4|11:4}} and study note). 

- *so that you will be a blessing:* This statement is a command and a promise in Hebrew. It depends on Abram obeying God's command ({{Genesis 12:1-3|12:1–3}}): “Go … so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you.”

- Because Abram obeyed the command to be a blessing ({{Genesis 12:2|12:2}}), God gave him three more promises. 

- *those who curse you:* People who ignored Abram and his covenant were rejecting God's choice and plan. 

- *all the families on earth will be blessed:* By faith, they could join the covenant God was making with Abram. The blessing spread worldwide through Abraham, Israel, the covenants, the prophets, Scripture, and the Messiah ({{Galatians 3:8|Galatians 3:8}}, {{Galatians 3:16|16}}; compare {{Romans 9:4-5|Romans 9:4–5}}).

Abram was middle-aged, settled, wealthy, and of high social status. He worshiped many gods (see study note on 11:27–32). When the Lord spoke to him ({{Genesis 12:1-3|12:1–3}}), he obediently left his old ways in Ur to follow God's plan. Because Abram responded in faith, God could confirm his promises ({{Genesis 12:2-3|12:2–3}}) in a binding covenant ({{Genesis 15:8-21|15:8–21}}).
Abram obeyed God's calling and followed his commands (see study note on 12:1–3). He traveled to Canaan ({{Genesis 12:4-6|12:4–6}}) and became a blessing ({{Genesis 12:5-9|12:5–9}}).
The* people* (Hebrew *hannepesh*, meaning "the lives") he brought into his household were probably converts. Abram first became a blessing by influencing his household to follow the Lord.

- *the Oak of Moreh*: This was probably a Canaanite shrine. Fertile groves were sacred to the Canaanites (compare {{Isaiah 1:29|Isaiah 1:29}}), and *Moreh* means "teacher." 

Abram proclaimed the Lord's name beside a pagan place of worship and instruction ({{Genesis 12:8|Genesis 12:8}}). 

- Abram continued to be a blessing by building an altar to worship God at Shechem and east of Bethel ({{Genesis 12:8|12:8}}).

- *the LORD appeared to Abram* at Shechem ({{Genesis 12:6|12:6}}) to confirm that this was the promised land. Israel was meant to live in this land, but they needed faith to share in God's promises (compare {{Numbers 14:1-45|Numbers 14}}; {{Joshua 1:6-9|Joshua 1:6–9}}). 

- *to your offspring:* Abram did not own the land yet. He lived there as a temporary settler.

*he called on the name of the LORD:* Calling on the name (identity and character) of the Lord is central to worship and witness (compare {{Genesis 4:26|4:26}}; see {{Exodus 34:5-7|Exodus 34:5–7}}). Abram needed to distinguish his sacrificial worship from that of the pagan Canaanites.
Abram had to keep moving camp because the Canaanites had the fertile land.
The Nile River supplied plenty of water for crops, so Egypt was usually the last area to experience famine.

- Abram's scheme came from fear, putting his family and God's promises at risk. He lacked faith when he went to Egypt. He stopped building altars, and deception became the main pattern of his behavior. Deception would trouble his family throughout Genesis ({{Genesis 26:1-11|26:1–11}}; {{Genesis 27:1-29|27:1–29}}; {{Genesis 29:15-30|29:15–30}}; {{Genesis 30:34-36|30:34–36}}; {{Genesis 31:6-11|31:6–11}}; {{Genesis 37:18-35|37:18–35}}; {{Genesis 39:7-20|39:7–20}}). 

- Abram's plan probably followed a custom where a brother arranged his sister's marriage (compare {{Genesis 24:29-61|24:29–61}}). Abram may have thought that any possible suitor would have to deal with him, giving him time to leave with Sarai. He did not expect Pharaoh to act without negotiation ({{Genesis 12:14-16|12:14–16}}).

- This story shows that God would allow Abram to put his promises at risk in this episode. Soon after Abram obeyed God’s call, a famine tested his weak faith. God rescued Abram and his family, even though Abram acted foolishly. In Egypt, he used deception instead of trusting God to protect him.

- This story intentionally mirrors Israel's later slavery in Egypt:

- Because of a famine (compare {{Genesis 12:10|Genesis 12:10}} with {{Genesis 47:13|Genesis 47:13}}), Abram and Israel went to Egypt (compare {{Genesis 12:10|Genesis 12:10}} with {{Genesis 47:27|Genesis 47:27}}). 

- There was an attempt to kill the males and save the females (compare {{Genesis 12:12|Genesis 12:12}} with {{Exodus 1:22|Exodus 1:22}}). 

- God sent plagues to Egypt (compare {{Genesis 12:17|Genesis 12:17}} with {{Exodus 7:14-11:10|Exodus 7:14–11:10}}). 

- Abram and Israel took riches from Egypt (compare {{Genesis 12:16|Genesis 12:16}} with {{Exodus 12:35-36|Exodus 12:35–36}}). 

- Pharaoh expelled them (Hebrew *shalakh*, meaning “send”; compare {{Genesis 12:19-20|Genesis 12:19–20}} with {{Exodus 12:31-33|Exodus 12:31–33}}) and they went to the Negev (compare {{Genesis 13:1|Genesis 13:1}} with {{Numbers 13:17|Numbers 13:17}}, {{Numbers 13:22|22}}). 

Israel was to believe that God would deliver them from bondage in Egypt through the plagues because their ancestor had already been rescued from bondage in Egypt.

*Please say you are my sister:* This request appears three times in Genesis (see also {{Genesis 20:2|20:2}}; {{Genesis 26:7|26:7}}). The text explains that this was Abram’s usual strategy ({{Genesis 20:13|20:13}}), and his son Isaac did the same thing. The first time this happened was outside the land, and the second time within it (chapter {{Genesis 20:1-18|20}}). This shows that God protected his promise in both regions.

Sarai was 65, but she would live to 127. If the biblical lifespans here are understood literally, she had lived only about half her life. By those standards, she may still have been at an age of full strength and maturity.

Sarai and Abram came from a noble family (see study note on 11:29), so she likely had a regal appearance and wore fine clothing. Pharaoh was drawn to both her beauty and the political advantage of an alliance with her family.

- Abram was bound by the king’s gift to an unwanted agreement about Sarai that he did not want and could not stop. His plan had put him in a dangerous situation. It put Abram, Sarai, and the promise at risk.

- Abram seemed to gain wealth from his deception, but these new possessions also led to new problems. Abram and Lot had to separate (chapter {{Genesis 13:1-18|13}}). Hagar, an Egyptian servant, later became the mother of Ishmael’s descendants (chapter {{Genesis 16:1-16|16}}). In the Bible, these descendants are often shown as being in conflict with Israel.
*Pharaoh* was a title for a ruler, not a personal name ({{Genesis 37:36|37:36}}; {{Exodus 1:15|Exodus 1:15}}).

God intervened to rescue Sarai and to preserve her marriage to Abram so that the covenant promise could be fulfilled. When Sarai was returned to Abram, Pharaoh rebuked him because of what had happened ({{Genesis 12:18-19|12:18–19}}).

Abram did not need to answer Pharaoh’s questions ({{Genesis 12:18-19|12:18–19}}) because Pharaoh’s rebuke was followed by expulsion. Pharaoh’s command echoed God’s command to Abram ({{Genesis 12:1|12:1}}), but Pharaoh’s words brought Abram shame and disgrace. Even so, God remained faithful and preserved his promise.

This story takes place during a time of conflict and God's blessings. At the beginning, Abram returns to a place where he had built an altar. The story emphasizes earlier events as Abram returns to the land ({{Genesis 13:3-4|13:3–4}}). Abram renews his worship and again calls on the Lord's name (see {{Genesis 12:8|12:8}}).
Abram already had powerful resources ({{Genesis 12:5|12:5}}). His time in Egypt increased his wealth and power ({{Genesis 12:16|12:16}}).

- Lot was also wealthy, owning many animals. Tents play an important role in Lot's story ({{Genesis 13:12|13:12}}). 

- The Canaanites and the Perizzites (see {{Genesis 34:30|34:30}}; {{Deuteronomy 7:1|Deuteronomy 7:1}}; {{Judges 1:4|Judges 1:4}}; {{Judges 3:5|3:5}}) controlled the fertile land. The argument between Abram's and Lot's herdsmen made Abram easier to attack.

Abram wanted to avoid conflict (Hebrew *meribah*) because they were close relatives (literally *brothers*). Later, Moses rebuked Israel for the incident in the wilderness at Meribah ({{Exodus 17:1-7|Exodus 17:1–7}}; {{Numbers 20:1-13|Numbers 20:1–13}}). He taught them to have faith in such situations. So, Meribah became a word of warning for testing and arguing with the Lord in unbelief (see {{Psalm 95:1-11|Psalm 95}}).

God promised the land to Abram. Abram might have told Lot to find his own place. Abram’s generosity showed his faith. He believed that even if he gave all the land away, God would still provide it to him and his descendants. Abram did not need to hold to things, while Lot's choices were selfish.

- What attracted Lot would not last. In the garden of the Lord, Adam and Eve gave in to their desire for what they saw. Later, Israel became enslaved in Egypt. Sodom and Gomorrah warn us about putting strong desires ahead of obedience to God ({{Genesis 3:5-6|Genesis 3:5–6}}; see {{1 John 2:16|1 John 2:16}}). 

- Zoar was a small town in the plain where Lot and his daughters later fled ({{Genesis 19:18-22|Genesis 19:18–22}}). Earlier, it was called Bela ({{Genesis 14:2|14:2}}).

- Lot's choice was completely selfish, showing no concern for Abram or faith in the Lord. 

- *the whole plain of the Jordan* (literally *the circle of the Jordan*): This was probably near the southern end of the Dead Sea, based on descriptions in ancient records that locate cities of the plain. This area is now very desolate.
The narrator makes many contrasts between Lot and Abram.
This suggests that Lot would not oppose Sodom's influence because he was focusing on his own interests.
Abram could give Lot the choice land because he believed in God’s promise. Abram waited for God to give him the land. Lot just took what he wanted.

- Hebron was an Anakite city ({{Numbers 13:22|Numbers 13:22}}) originally called Kiriath-arba (meaning “city of Arba”). It was located in the forested highlands just north of the Negev ({{Genesis 12:9|Genesis 12:9}}; {{Joshua 17:15|Joshua 17:15}}). Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob all settled there ({{Genesis 18:1|Genesis 18:1}}; {{Genesis 35:27|35:27}}; {{Genesis 37:14|37:14}}). Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah were buried in Hebron ({{Genesis 23:19|23:19}}; {{Genesis 35:27-29|35:27–29}}; {{Genesis 49:29-32|49:29–32}}; {{Genesis 50:13|50:13}}). 

- Mamre was an Amorite ({{Genesis 14:13|14:13}}; {{Genesis 15:16|15:16}}).
Tidal apparently ruled several city-states. The text calls his people *Goiim*, which means “nations” in Hebrew.

Archaeology has not identified these kings. But ancient texts include similar names, which supports the report’s reliability. The Mesopotamian kings were allies under one leading ruler, likely Amraphel, who is named first.
In this typical ancient political conflict, powerful kings allied to control smaller dependent states.

King Chedorlaomer seems to have defeated the kings of the Siddim Valley earlier and made them pay tribute in asphalt, olive oil, and copper. In the thirteenth year, they stopped paying. In the fourteenth year ({{Genesis 14:5|14:5}}), the invading kings returned to bring them under their rule again.

This was Chedorlaomer’s war. Under the feudal system of tribal affiliations, those in covenant with him had to fight. It was also Abram’s battle to rescue Lot, and those under treaty with him had to accompany him.
The invaders came down the King’s Highway on the east side of the Jordan Valley to the Gulf of Aqaba, then circled back to the valley of the Dead Sea.

The five cities of the Plain were close together near the south end of the Dead Sea. The Mesopotamian kings crushed the weak revolt, plundered Sodom and Gomorrah, and carried Lot away with the other captives.

- The word *Hebrew* appears here for the first time in the Bible. It is different from the later term *Habiru* found in Egyptian texts. The Habiru were hired soldiers who roamed the land during the time of the judges. 

- *Mamre:* See study note on 13:18. 

- *a brother*: Or *ally.*

- *Abram … mobilized the 318 trained men born in his household: *This shows that Abram was a strong leader and that God’s promise to make him great was already being fulfilled ({{Genesis 12:2-3|Genesis 12:2–3}}). 

- Dan was a city about 241 kilometers (150 miles) north of Abram’s home in Hebron. At that time, the city was called Laish or Leshem (see {{Joshua 19:47|Joshua 19:47}} and study note; {{Judges 18:29|Judges 18:29}}). Dan, the son whose descendants later settled there during the time of the judges, had not yet been born ({{Genesis 30:6|Genesis 30:6}}; {{Judges 18:1-29|Judges 18:1–29}}). It seems that an editor later updated the place name so that later audiences would know which city the text meant.

God could give his people victory over any forces invading the promised land. Faithfulness to God was necessary for victory. God promises to bless his people and give them victory over the world. He uses those who respond to his call and can skillfully use weapons of war.
Damascus was 64 kilometers (40 miles) north of Dan. Hobah was 97 kilometers (about 60 miles) north of Damascus.
The Valley of Shaveh, or King’s Valley, was probably the Kidron Valley (see {{2 Samuel 18:18|2 Samuel 18:18}}).

- The name *Melchizedek* means “king of righteousness.” This suggests the king of Salem was a righteous servant of God. He was probably a Jebusite priest and king. Later writers regarded him as a type of Christ, that is, a person who points forward to Christ ({{Psalm 110:4|Psalm 110:4}}; {{Hebrews 7:1-19|Hebrews 7:1–19}}). 

- *Salem* is the ancient name for Jerusalem (compare {{Psalm 76:2|Psalm 76:2}}).
By giving a tenth of everything to Melchizedek, Abram acknowledged Melchizedek as spiritual authority (see {{Hebrews 7:4|Hebrews 7:4}}). He affirmed that God had given him victory.

Abram understood that accepting the king of Sodom's offer (see study note on 14:1–2) might make him an ally or subject, as Lot had been. This could put God’s promises at risk. Faith looks beyond the world’s riches to the greater blessings that God will give.

In this oath, Abram may have been making it clear that his God, the LORD (Yahweh), is the same as God Most High, whom Melchizedek spoke about. It is possible that Melchizedek did not know the name Yahweh.

- *Do not be afraid:* Abram did not have a son to inherit his property. The Lord addressed Abram’s anxiety about the future with comforting words.

- *I am your shield:* The Hebrew word for *shield *(*magen*) comes from the same root word as Melchizedek's word *delivered* ({{Genesis 14:20|14:20}}). The Lord, who had delivered Abram's enemies into his power, would continue to protect him. 

- *your very great reward:* The promise of children was still unfulfilled ({{Genesis 12:2-3|12:2–3}}; see also {{Psalm 127:3|Psalm 127:3}}).

God made a covenant (a special agreement) with Abram. In this covenant, God confirmed the promises he had made earlier when he summoned Abram to leave his country ({{Genesis 12:1-3|12:1–3}}). Abram's descendants would experience a long period of slavery before God made these promises come true.

In Genesis chapter 15 God repeated his promises to give Abram land and a large family. He did this by making a covenant with Abram. But Sarai hadn’t yet had any children. So Abram didn’t understand how God would make his family into a great nation. Even so, Abram believed God’s promise to give him a son.

Abram’s faith pleased God. Abram was made right with God by believing in God. This is also called being made righteous or being justified. God put his covenant with Abram into effect through the sacrifice of animals.

In Genesis chapter 17 God repeated his covenant with Abram. He changed Abram and Sarai’s names to Abraham and Sarah. He explained that his covenant with Abraham’s family would last for ever. The sign of the covenant was circumcision. God’s promise of a son took a long time to happen. Because of this it was hard for Abraham and Sarah to fully trust God.

Abraham had a son with Sarah’s slave named Hagar. Abraham lied to the king of Gerar about his wife Sarah. Sarah laughed and didn’t believe God’s promise that she would have a child. But God made it clear that Abraham and Sarah would be the parents of a son.

The three men who visited them said that their son Isaac would be born within a year. God would continue the covenant through Isaac. Even though Abraham and Sarah didn’t fully trust him, God protected them. He also protected the people close to them. He protected Hagar in the desert and promised to bless Ishmael. He also rescued Lot when Sodom and Gomorrah were destroyed.

Abram used wordplay to show his concern that Eliezer of Damascus (Hebrew *dammeseq*), a man in Abram's household, would become his heir (Hebrew ben-mesheq, which means “son of possession”). This was the usual practice when a man had no son.

God confirmed that the promise to Abram was for his own children. Then God showed Abram the stars as a sign of the many descendants he would have ({{Genesis 22:17|22:17}}; {{Genesis 26:4|26:4}}). The apostle Paul quotes this promise in {{Romans 4:18|Romans 4:18}} to emphasize Abram’s strong faith.

- *Abram believed:* God made a covenant with someone who trusted in him. The text does not say when Abram first believed. The Hebrew text does not link Abram's belief to the promise about the stars. It simply says that *Abram believed the LORD*. Abram already had faith. Leaving Ur was his first major act that showed it (see {{Hebrews 11:8-10|Hebrews 11:8–10}}). 

- *it was credited to him as righteousness:* The New Testament quotes this key statement about Abram's faith three times ({{Romans 4:3|Romans 4:3}}; {{Galatians 3:6|Galatians 3:6}}; {{James 2:23|James 2:23}}). The New Testament writers use this verse to support the teaching that God makes a person right with himself through trust in him (see also {{Romans 4:22-23|Romans 4:22–23}}).
In a special ceremony, God made a covenant with Abram and promised to do what he had said.

Obeying God's instructions, Abram collected three herd animals for the ceremony and cut them in half. Cutting the animals symbolized the oath. It showed that the person making the covenant risked his own life if he did not keep his promise ({{Jeremiah 34:18|Jeremiah 34:18}}).
*birds of prey:* These are ceremonially unclean birds that symbolize those who unjustly attack Abraham's heirs ({{Genesis 15:13-14|15:13–14}}).

- *mistreated:* The same word appears in {{Exodus 1:11-12|Exodus 1:11–12}}. Egypt, like "birds of prey" ({{Genesis 15:11|Genesis 15:11}}), tried to destroy Israel and stop the fulfillment of the covenant. 

- *four hundred years: *This is probably an approximate number (also {{Acts 7:6|Acts 7:6}}; compare {{Exodus 12:40|Exodus 12:40}}; {{Galatians 3:17|Galatians 3:17}}). According to the Hebrew text's timeline, the family moved to Egypt around 1876 BC. The exodus happened around 1446 BC, but many scholars believe the Israelites left Egypt later, around 1270 BC (see Exodus Book Introduction, “The Date of the Exodus”).
Not even 400 years of slavery could interfere with God’s plan to fulfill the covenant.

- The reasons for Israel’s bondage included God’s justice. God would tolerate the sins of the Amorites until they fully deserved judgment. 

- *is not yet complete:* To give the promised land to Israel, God would justly remove those living in the land. Fulfilling promises to Israel also meant judgment for the people in the land. But if they trusted in him, God would save individual people (see {{Joshua 2:1-15|Joshua 2:1–15}}; {{Joshua 6:23-25|6:23–25}}; {{Hebrews 11:31|Hebrews 11:31}}; {{James 2:25|James 2:25}}). Until then, God would send Jacob's family to Egypt so Israel could become a great nation. Seeing this future frightened Abram ({{Genesis 15:12|Genesis 15:12}}). But it was comforting to know nothing could stop God's plan.

*smoking firepot and a flaming torch:* Fire represented the Lord's cleansing and consuming zeal. It also represented how no one could come near him because of his holiness (compare {{Isaiah 6:3-7|Isaiah 6:3–7}}). The holy God made (literally *cut*) a one-sided covenant with Abram. The promises were absolutely certain. This was because they did not rely on what Abram or his descendants' might do.

God clearly defined the borders of the promised land (the land he promised to give). He told Abram that even though there would be death and suffering, including slavery, he and his descendants would still receive these promises. God confirmed this with an oath (see {{Hebrews 6:13-14|Hebrews 6:13–14}}). Nothing can separate God’s people from his love or stop the fulfillment (the bringing about) of his plans (see {{Romans 8:18-39|Romans 8:18–39}}; {{2 Peter 1:3-4|2 Peter 1:3–4}}).

Abram and Sarai dealt with the stress of Sarai not being able to have children and being too old to give birth. 

According to the custom in that culture, a woman unable to have children could give her servant as a secondary wife to her husband. The child from this union became the primary wife's child. They adopted the child as the heir. 

Sarai's suggestion was acceptable according to the culture's custom. But it was a human plan that showed a lack of faith in God. God’s promises would be fulfilled by faith.
While they waited for their promised son to be born, Abram and Sarai tried another plan. This plan did not show trust in God.
Hagar might have thought Abram would favor her instead of Sarai (compare {{Proverbs 30:21-23|Proverbs 30:21–23}}).

*the angel of the LORD:* The angel of the Lord was the Lord himself in some passages ({{Genesis 16:13|16:13}}; {{Genesis 21:17|21:17}}; {{Genesis 22:11-12|22:11–12}}; {{Genesis 31:11-13|31:11–13}}; {{Genesis 48:16|48:16}}; {{Exodus 3:2|Exodus 3:2}}; {{Exodus 32:34|32:34}}; {{Judges 6:11|Judges 6:11}}, {{Judges 6:16|16}}, {{Judges 6:22|22}}; {{Judges 13:22-23|13:22–23}}; {{Zechariah 3:1-2|Zechariah 3:1–2}}). But in other passages he is distinct from the Lord ({{Genesis 24:7|Genesis 24:7}}; {{2 Samuel 24:16|2 Samuel 24:16}}; {{Zechariah 1:12|Zechariah 1:12}}). 

This figure is often understood as a *theophany* (a visible appearance of God) or a *Christophany* (an appearance of the Messiah before he became human (see {{Genesis 18:1-2|Genesis 18:1–2}}; {{Genesis 19:1|19:1}}; {{Numbers 22:22|Numbers 22:22}}; {{Judges 2:1-4|Judges 2:1–4}}; {{Judges 5:23|5:23}}; {{Zechariah 12:8|Zechariah 12:8}}). In these cases, he speaks with the authority of the Lord himself.

The angel asked Hagar questions that helped her speak openly to God. When she did, God told her to return and submit to Sarai ({{Genesis 16:9|16:9}}). He also promised that her son would have many descendants, so many that they could not be counted.

The angel of the Lord did not call Hagar Abram’s wife. Instead, he called her Sarai’s servant. Hagar would bear Abram’s child, but Ishmael was not part of God’s covenant with Abram.

Hagar’s son would become the father of a large nation. This nation would be strong but often hostile, living in the Arabian Desert and frequently in conflict with Israel (compare {{Genesis 25:18|25:18}}). 

God blessed Ishmael as Abram's descendant. But God did not choose Ishmael to continue the covenant. God kept that blessing for Abram's heir based on God's promise.

Names in Genesis often emphasize the message of a passage. They help the people of God remember the events and their importance in the history of faith. The name *Ishmael* means "God hears." It marks the moment when *the LORD … heard* Hagar's cry of distress (see also study note on 16:14–15). This name would have greatly comforted Hagar. God listened to her prayers and acknowledged her complaint.

- Hagar showed faith in God through her words and obedience. 

- *the God who sees me:* God understood Hagar's situation and protected her.

The name *Beer-lahai-roi *means “well of the Living One who sees me.” This name and *Ishmael* were a message and a rebuke for Abram and Sarai (see {{Genesis 16:11|16:11}}). God notices suffering and listens to those crying out in need. 

Sarai and Abram should have prayed instead of trying to fulfill the promise themselves by following a social custom (compare {{Genesis 25:21|25:21}}). Giving children to a woman who cannot have them is God's work ({{Psalm 113:9|Psalm 113:9}}; compare {{1 Samuel 1:1-28|1 Samuel 1:1–28}}; {{Luke 1:1-25|Luke 1:1–25}}). Humans cannot solve impossible problems. The Lord hears those who suffer, sees their needs, and will provide for them in miraculous ways.

- *God Almighty *(Hebrew* El-Shaddai*): This name for God emphasizes his power (see also {{Genesis 28:3|28:3}}; {{Genesis 35:11|35:11}}; {{Genesis 43:14|43:14}}; {{Genesis 48:3|48:3}}; {{Genesis 49:25|49:25}}). 

- *Walk before Me and be blameless:* To bless the nations, Abram needed to obey. Almighty God would guide his actions.

God gave Abram's family signs that his promises would come true. He changed Abram's name to Abraham ({{Genesis 17:1-8|17:1–8}}). He established circumcision as the sign of the covenant ({{Genesis 17:9-14|17:9–14}}, {{Genesis 17:23-27|23–27}}). He changed Sarai's name to Sarah ({{Genesis 17:15-22|17:15–22}}).

God guaranteed his promise by changing Abram’s name. *Abram* means “exalted father.” This referred to his father Terah and his noble lineage ({{Genesis 11:27|11:27}}). His new name, *Abraham* (Hebrew *’ab hamon*), means "father of a multitude." This was a wordplay on the promise of his countless descendants (see also {{John 8:31-59|John 8:31–59}}; {{Romans 4:16-17|Romans 4:16–17}}; {{Galatians 3:7|Galatians 3:7}}, {{Galatians 3:15-19|15–19}}, {{Galatians 3:29|29}}). Whenever the new name was used, he and his household would remember that a multitude of nations would come from him.

*kings will descend from you:* This is the first sign that Israel would become a nation ruled by kings (see also {{Genesis 35:11|35:11}}; {{Genesis 36:31|36:31}}; {{Numbers 24:7|Numbers 24:7}}; {{Deuteronomy 17:14-18|Deuteronomy 17:14–18}}; {{Deuteronomy 28:36|28:36}}).

The land of Canaan was to be an everlasting possession for the descendants of Abraham. The Lord would always be their God (see {{Jeremiah 31:31-40|Jeremiah 31:31–40}}; {{Zechariah 8:8|Zechariah 8:8}}; {{Luke 1:68-79|Luke 1:68–79}}; {{Revelation 21:1-4|Revelation 21:1–4}}).
God gave circumcision as a confirming sign that reminded all households of loyalty to the covenant.

*will be cut off:* This punishment seems to have several applications. A person could be exiled from society or put to death by the community; most often it warned that a person might die prematurely (see {{Exodus 31:14|Exodus 31:14}}; {{Leviticus 7:20-27|Leviticus 7:20–27}}; {{Leviticus 17:3-4|17:3–4}}; {{Leviticus 20:17-18|20:17–18}}; {{Leviticus 23:28-29|23:28–29}}; {{Numbers 15:30-31|Numbers 15:30–31}}; see also {{Psalm 31:22|Psalm 31:22}}; {{Ezekiel 21:4|Ezekiel 21:4}}; {{Romans 9:3|Romans 9:3}}; {{Romans 11:22|11:22}}). 

Failure to be circumcised was a serious violation of the covenant (see {{Exodus 4:24-26|Exodus 4:24–26}}; compare {{Galatians 5:2-4|Galatians 5:2–4}}).
Sarah’s new name marked an important step in her calling (God’s purpose for her life). It fit her role as the future mother of kings and pointed to God’s promise.
*he laughed* (Hebrew *yitskhaq*): This was because the promise seemed unbelievable. He thought his family line would continue through Ishmael. But Abraham and Sarah would have their own son.

The name *Isaac* (Hebrew* yitskhaq*) means “he laughs.” This recalls Abraham's disbelief when he heard God's promise. It also reminds us of God's favor and pleasure at Isaac's birth (compare {{Genesis 21:6|21:6}}).
God would not abandon Ishmael. His family would prosper (see {{Genesis 25:13-16|25:13–16}}). But the covenant promises were for Isaac.

After God spoke to Abraham about Isaac, Abraham followed God's instructions immediately. He performed circumcision as a sign of faith, showing their participation in the covenant (compare {{Romans 4:11-12|Romans 4:11–12}}; {{Galatians 5:2-6|Galatians 5:2–6}}, {{Galatians 5:11|11}}; {{Galatians 6:15|6:15}}; {{Philippians 3:2-3|Philippians 3:2–3}}; {{Colossians 2:11-12|Colossians 2:11–12}}; {{1 Peter 3:21|1 Peter 3:21}}).

The Lord's visit to Abraham set the time for Isaac's birth. The three visitors were probably the Lord and two angels (see study note on 16:7). Abraham welcomed the visitors peacefully and generously, which contrasted with the chaos and corruption in Sodom (chapter {{Genesis 19:1-38|19}}). 

Sharing a meal was important for making or confirming covenants. When God was ready to fulfill the covenant promise, he personally shared a meal with Abraham. Fellowship with God has always included a communal meal (see {{Exodus 24:9-11|Exodus 24:9–11}}; {{Matthew 26:17-30|Matthew 26:17–30}} *//* {{Luke 22:7-38|Luke 22:7–38}}; {{Acts 2:42|Acts 2:42}}; {{1 Corinthians 11:20-34|1 Corinthians 11:20–34}}).
Abraham received his visitors as very important guests, perhaps realizing that they were messengers from God.

*My lord:* The Hebrew text uses *’adonay*, which always refers to God. In Hebrew tradition, people said this word when they saw the letters of God's holy name ("Yahweh") in the text. The text here might use *’adonay* instead of the more common *’adoni* to show this was the angel of the Lord, meaning the Lord himself (see study note on 16:7). We do not know if Abraham knew who his visitors were at first. But by the end of the story, he knew he had been talking with God.
The visitors asked about Sarah by name, even though no one had told them who she was.
*I will surely return: *The Hebrew phrase is emphatic. The statement announced a certain promise and dramatic change.

Sarah thought no one noticed her disbelieving laughter. But God knows what people do in secret and what they feel (see {{Psalm 69:5|Psalm 69:5}}; {{Proverbs 20:27|Proverbs 20:27}}; {{Mark 4:22|Mark 4:22}}; {{Luke 8:43-48|Luke 8:43–48}}; {{Hebrews 4:13|Hebrews 4:13}}). He knows if they doubt promises or trust in him (see {{Hebrews 11:11-12|Hebrews 11:11–12}}).

*Is anything too difficult for the LORD?: *This question does not expect an answer. It teaches that nothing is too difficult for God.

God can do great and surprising things. For those who live in covenant (a binding promise relationship) with him, nothing is impossible, because nothing is too hard for the Lord.

God trusted Abraham as his prophet ({{Genesis 18:16-21|18:16–21}}; see {{Genesis 20:7|20:7}}). In return, Abraham pleaded that God would save Sodom ({{Genesis 18:23-32|18:23–32}}; see {{Hebrews 7:23-26|Hebrews 7:23–26}}). God can do anything he wants. This passage confirms it will be fair and right.

Abraham was responsible for teaching his descendants to be righteous and act justly so they might enjoy God's blessings. It was important for Abraham to know how God’s righteousness was at work in judgment.

God, who knows everything, was cautious in his judgment. He knew the sins of Sodom and Gomorrah. This careful examination showed God's justice in a way humans could understand. He would not destroy the people unless he was certain they were wicked.

Abraham probably thought there were more righteous people in Sodom and Gomorrah than there were (see study note on 19:14). Concerned for them, he made a legal appeal to the Lord based on God's justice. His prayer might seem bold, as if he were negotiating with God. But he approached God with true humility and respect. He did not try to convince God to act against his will. Instead, he prayed for the well-being of others (compare with Lot’s prayer, {{Genesis 19:18-23|19:18–23}}). 

God is a fair judge. "Righteousness exalts a nation" ({{Proverbs 14:34|Proverbs 14:34}}). Righteous people help preserve society (compare {{Matthew 5:13|Matthew 5:13}}).

- The two angels also first appeared to Abraham as men ({{Genesis 18:2|18:2}}). 

- Lot was no longer living in tents near Sodom ({{Genesis 13:12|13:12}}). He had become a citizen and leader in Sodom, sitting at the city entrance. Community leaders (elders) usually gathered at the gates. This is where they publicly finalized legal and business matters (compare {{Genesis 23:18|23:18}}; {{Job 29:7|Job 29:7}}, {{Job 29:12-17|12–17}}). 

As a righteous man, Lot tried to guide the people of Sodom to live better lives ({{2 Peter 2:7-8|2 Peter 2:7–8}}; compare {{Genesis 19:9|Genesis 19:9}}). While he opposed their evil behavior, Lot still chose Sodom’s wealthy lifestyle over the simpler life in the hills (compare {{Genesis 13:10-11|13:10–11}}). Life in the hills offered fewer temptations and less corruption but lacked the comforts of Sodom. 

As long as the Lord left Lot and his family alone in Sodom, he lived comfortably and kept his belief in God. But, he could not continue living this way. Sodom would have destroyed Lot if the Lord had not destroyed Sodom. 

- This story showed Israel that God is the righteous judge of the whole earth ({{Genesis 18:25|18:25}}). He punishes evil fairly. In evil societies, wrongdoing leads to unfair treatment and suffering for others.

The two angels who were with the Lord at Mamre (compare {{Genesis 18:2|18:2}}, {{Genesis 18:22|22}}) went on to Sodom. They knew the people there were very wicked. Even though Lot welcomed them, they first chose to stay in the public square instead of going into his house.

The Canaanites were evil people who tried to corrupt others. God judged their immoral civilization and warned others not to be like them. It was difficult to get Lot and his family out of Sodom. But it was even more difficult to remove Sodom's influence from them. 

This chapter helped later Israelites understand the moral and spiritual dangers of the people living in and around the promised land. This included the Canaanites and Lot’s descendants, the Moabites and the Ammonites (see {{Numbers 22:1-25:18|Numbers 22–25}}; {{Deuteronomy 23:3-6|Deuteronomy 23:3–6}}; {{Joshua 24:9|Joshua 24:9}}; {{Judges 10:7-9|Judges 10:7–9}}; {{Judges 11:4-5|11:4–5}}; {{1 Samuel 10:27|1 Samuel 10:27}}; {{1 Kings 11:1-3|1 Kings 11:1–3}}; {{2 Kings 24:2|2 Kings 24:2}}).

The evil actions of the men of the city were matched by the hypocrisy of Lot ({{Genesis 19:6-9|19:6–9}}). The men acted in a wicked and violent way toward Lot’s visitors. Lot tried to protect his guests. However, he offered his daughters to the crowd instead. This action showed serious moral failure.

Lot strongly opposed the men’s plan to harm his guests. He spoke against their wicked actions. However, he wrongly offered his daughters to protect the visitors, which showed a serious moral failure.

At first, Lot had only set up his tent near Sodom. Over time, he became closely tied to the city, and its influence shaped his life.
The men of the city became enraged because Lot tried to stop their evil behavior. It was amazing to them that Lot would judge them, since he apparently had not done so before.
Lot’s warning words were not taken seriously because of his hypocrisy. It seemed that there would not be even ten righteous people in the city.

- Lot escaped God's judgment because of God's grace, but Lot was still hesitant to leave Sodom. Israel would forever remember Lot as someone who hesitated and needed angels to pull him to safety. The Lord was merciful and spared Lot because of Abraham ({{Genesis 18:23|18:23}}; {{Genesis 19:29|19:29}}).

- Today, people who follow God often feel pressure to copy the wrong ways that many people live. God asks his followers to live differently from people who do not follow him. This means Christians should choose actions and behaviors that show they belong to God ({{1 John 2:15-17|1 John 2:15–17}}). God will judge the corrupt systems of the world. This judgment will be even more severe than the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah ({{Matthew 11:23-24|Matthew 11:23–24}}).
Lot asked the angels for permission to live in the small town of Zoar (which means "little place") even after they saved him.

Compare {{Luke 17:29|Luke 17:29}}. The eruption of Mount Vesuvius, the volcano that destroyed Pompeii in AD 79, along with more recent natural disasters, shows how quickly a complete disaster like this can happen.

*looked back:* The verb form indicates intense gazing at the world she loved, not just a curious look ({{Genesis 15:5|15:5}}; {{Exodus 33:8|Exodus 33:8}}; {{Numbers 21:9|Numbers 21:9}}; {{1 Samuel 2:32|1 Samuel 2:32}}; compare {{Exodus 3:6|Exodus 3:6}}). Lot’s wife had become too attached to Sodom to follow God's calling. So God judged her as she lingered on the valley slopes. 

Christ’s return to judge the world will be as sudden and devastating as Sodom's destruction ({{Luke 17:32-37|Luke 17:32–37}}). Those who desire the life of this wicked world will lose both this world and the next.

God listened to Abraham's plea (compare {{Genesis 18:23-32|18:23–32}}). But Lot lost everything during the destruction of Sodom. His choice to live in the fertile land of Sodom eventually led him into a dangerous situation ({{Genesis 13:10-13|13:10–13}}). After this, he could no longer remain in the land he had chosen.

Sodom's culture apparently influenced Lot’s daughters more than their father's values. They had no issues having children with their drunk father because they saw no other way to continue their family line (see {{Genesis 9:21-22|9:21–22}}).

The poverty of the cave contrasts with the wealth Lot shared with Abram and the good life he lived in Sodom. Abraham would father a righteous nation ({{Genesis 17:1|17:1}}), but Lot and his daughters started a new Sodom.

- The daughters' plan worked. They each became pregnant by their father. From these two sons, born from incest, came two of Israel's long-time enemies: the nations of Moab and Ammon. Their extreme wickedness was partly due to their origins. 

- Both daughters chose descriptive names for their sons. *Moab* means "from my father" and *Ben-ammi* means "son of my people." These names subtly hinted at their actions without making people suspicious who were unaware of the stories.
Gerar was near the coast in Philistine land, about 19 kilometers (12 miles) south of Gaza and 80 kilometers (50 miles) southwest of Hebron.

- This second "sister story" in Genesis (compare {{Genesis 12:10-20|12:10–20}}) happened just before Sarah became pregnant with Isaac (chapter {{Genesis 21:1-34|21}}). In both instances, God protected Abraham and Sarah's marriage to keep it pure for the covenant promises. To be part of God's plan, his people must separate from worldly corruption. 

- This story happened in the promised land. It showed Israel how God intervened in people's lives to fulfill his plan. He protected them from threats from other tribes. He used his chosen people to mediate his relationship with other nations. 

- By preventing adultery from destroying Abraham's marriage, God reminded the Israelites not to marry those who would lead them away from the Lord ({{Ezra 9:1-4|Ezra 9:1–4}}; {{Nehemiah 13:23-27|Nehemiah 13:23–27}}; {{Malachi 2:10-17|Malachi 2:10–17}}). They should not allow any chance for temptation. Adultery would eventually destroy the covenant and the people.

- Abraham lied to Abimelech, just as he had lied to Pharaoh ({{Genesis 12:13|12:13}}). Isaac later did the same ({{Genesis 26:1-11|26:1–11}}), probably learning this from his father.

- *Abimelech* (which means "my father the king") was probably a title like *Pharaoh* ({{Genesis 37:36|37:36}}; {{Exodus 1:15|Exodus 1:15}}), not a personal name (see study note on Genesis 26:1).
*One night … God came … in a dream:* God urgently intervened to stop Abimelech from harming Sarah's purity right before fulfilling his promise ({{Genesis 18:10|18:10}}; {{Genesis 21:1-3|21:1–3}}).

God gave Abimelech a strong warning against committing adultery. This was a crime that could be punished by death (compare {{Exodus 20:14|Exodus 20:14}}). The ancient Near East considered it "tremendous guilt" ({{Genesis 20:9|Genesis 20:9}}).

- Abimelech was innocent ({{Genesis 20:6|20:6}}). He knew of no wrong he had done. But he was close to committing adultery. Not knowing the truth does not remove guilt ({{Leviticus 4:13-14|Leviticus 4:13–14}}). 

- *would You destroy a nation even though it is innocent?:* Abimelech's plea to God echoes Abraham's earlier words (compare {{Genesis 18:23-32|18:23–32}}). It shows Abraham's lack of faith at this time.

Because Abimelech acted with a clear conscience, God kept him from sinning. God will graciously help those who try to do what is right. When people act with reverence toward God, God gives them more revelation and draws them into more specific faith (see {{Acts 10:1-48|Acts 10}}).

Abraham's prayer saved the king's life and restored his family ({{Genesis 20:17-18|20:17–18}}). Abimelech learned that Abraham's God was sovereign (meaning God has complete power and authority over everything). Abraham, as God's prophet, received God's messages and would pray for others (see {{Numbers 12:13|Numbers 12:13}}; {{Deuteronomy 9:20|Deuteronomy 9:20}}). This was true even if he did not always act like a prophet.

Abraham received rebukes from Abimelech and God (compare {{Genesis 12:17-19|12:17–19}}). Abimelech was upset because Abraham's lie made him guilty of this serious sin (see study note on 20:3–7). Abimelech understood that taking a married woman into his harem (a group of wives and concubines) was wrong.

Abraham's deceit was not just a brief loss of faith. Even after being scolded in Egypt, he used this strategy everywhere he traveled (compare {{Genesis 12:12-13|12:12–13}}). Living by faith requires perseverance.

Abimelech showed he was an honorable person by making things right (see study note on 20:4–5). He made things right by letting Abraham live in the area. He also gave him slaves, livestock (compare {{Genesis 21:27|21:27}}), and 1,000 pieces of silver to make up for any wrong done to Sarah.

The inability to have children suggests that some time had passed. God controls births. He decides when women can have children ({{Genesis 25:21|25:21}}; {{Genesis 29:31|29:31}}; {{Genesis 30:2|30:2}}, {{Genesis 30:17|17}}, {{Genesis 30:22-23|22–23}}; {{1 Samuel 1:19-20|1 Samuel 1:19–20}}; {{Psalm 113:9|Psalms 113:9}}; {{Psalm 127:3|127:3}}; {{Luke 1:13|Luke 1:13}}).
